cls.banner: The Green New Deal resolution states an opinion of the House of Representatives. Even if adopted, it would not change federal law, direct any agency or spend any money, and it would not be sent to the Senate or the President.
cls.checks: This analysis does not run its loophole, enforcement and funding checks on the Green New Deal resolution, because the resolution imposes no obligation that could be enforced. The analysis instead compares the resolution's stated goals to its legal effect and sets out what a binding version would have to contain.
purpose.ladder.mechanism: The resolution would put the House on record that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
purpose.ladder.outcome: The resolution would establish a shared framework of climate and economic goals against which later bills can be measured.
purpose.ladder.aim: The resolution's stated aim is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, millions of jobs and greater economic security, achieved through a ten-year national mobilization.
promises.0.p: The title of the Green New Deal resolution states that it recognizes a duty of the federal government to create a Green New Deal.
promises.0.why: Adoption would record the House's opinion that a federal duty to create a Green New Deal exists. A simple resolution has no power to create a legal duty.
promises.1.p: Paragraph (1)(A) of the Green New Deal resolution states net-zero greenhouse gas emissions as the resolution's first goal.
promises.1.why: Net-zero emissions is stated only as a goal. No provision of the resolution caps, prices or regulates greenhouse gas emissions, and the resolving clause gives no date for reaching net-zero.
promises.2.p: News coverage described the Green New Deal resolution as seeking to eliminate U.S. greenhouse gas emissions within a decade.
promises.2.why: Paragraph (2) of the resolving clause states that the goals "should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization". The resolution does not say when the ten years begin or that net-zero emissions must be reached by their end.
promises.3.p: A 2023 Senate press release described the Green New Deal resolution as directing Congress to act.
promises.3.why: A resolution expressing the sense of a chamber states an opinion. It cannot direct Congress, a committee or an agency to do anything.
promises.4.p: Paragraphs (1)(B) and (4)(H) of the Green New Deal resolution call for millions of good, high-wage jobs and for guaranteeing a job to all people of the United States.
promises.4.why: The resolution creates no program, agency, eligibility rule or funding for the jobs it describes or for the job guarantee.
promises.5.p: Paragraph (2)(C) of the Green New Deal resolution calls for meeting 100 percent of U.S. power demand through clean, renewable and zero-emission energy sources.
promises.5.why: The 100 percent clean power goal has no standard, no deadline and no definition of which energy sources qualify.
questions.0.q: What would be legally different the day after the House adopted the Green New Deal resolution?
questions.0.a: Nothing would be legally different. A simple resolution speaks for one chamber, is not sent to the Senate or the President, and has no force of law. The Congressional Research Service notes that agencies may still watch such measures as a signal of what Congress might do later.
questions.1.q: For each goal in the Green New Deal resolution, which words in the resolution would deliver it?
questions.1.a: None of the Green New Deal resolution's goals is paired with an operative provision. The resolution's governing verbs are "it is the duty", "should be accomplished" and "will require". The resolution names no agency, makes no appropriation and amends no statute.
questions.2.q: Even read only as a statement of goals, where does the wording of the Green New Deal resolution leave room for differing interpretations?
questions.2.a: Four of the resolution's emissions goals are qualified by as far as is "technologically feasible". The net-zero goal has no date in the resolving clause. The phrase "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy is not defined, so the resolution does not settle whether nuclear power or fossil generation with carbon capture counts.
questions.3.q: Which agency or official does the Green New Deal resolution assign to carry out its goals?
questions.3.a: The resolution assigns its duty only to "the Federal Government" as a whole. It names no department, agency, official or committee.
questions.4.q: What would the Green New Deal resolution cost, and where would the money come from?
questions.4.a: The Green New Deal resolution contains no cost figure and provides no funding. Because it has no budgetary effect, no official cost estimate would be prepared for it.
questions.5.q: Has the text of the Green New Deal resolution ever been voted on in Congress?
questions.5.a: The House has not voted on the resolution. The Senate majority leader introduced the same text as a joint resolution, and on March 26, 2019 a motion to take it up failed with 0 votes in favor, 57 against and 43 senators voting present.
questions.6.q: Do binding bills exist that would carry out parts of the Green New Deal resolution's framework?
questions.6.a: Binding bills of that kind exist. Sponsors have introduced separate bills, including a Green New Deal for Public Housing Act and Civilian Climate Corps legislation, and a bill to establish a Green New Deal for public schools was introduced in July 2026. Those bills, not the resolution, are the vehicles to which loophole analysis applies.
questions.7.q: What would a binding version of the Green New Deal resolution's first goal, net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, need to contain?
questions.7.a: A binding net-zero measure would need a statutory emissions target with dates, a named agency with authority to set and enforce limits, a funding source, and a way to enforce the target against the government itself. The "binding version" table in the bigger picture panel sets out these requirements goal by goal.
findings.G1.title: The Green New Deal resolution expresses the sense of the House of Representatives and, if adopted, would have no force of law.
findings.G1.plain: The resolving clause of the Green New Deal resolution begins with the words "it is the sense of the House of Representatives", which mean the House is stating a view. Nothing that follows those words can require any person or agency to act, whatever the language says.
findings.G1.tech: The Green New Deal resolution is a simple resolution, which is adopted by one chamber and is not presented to the President. The Congressional Research Service describes sense-of measures as not legally binding. Every paragraph of the resolving clause depends grammatically on the sense-of-the-House clause.
findings.G1.use: A member of Congress can cite a vote for, or cosponsorship of, the Green New Deal resolution as action on climate even though no law has changed.
findings.G1.inq.q: What happened to the Green New Deal resolution in Congress, and what does that history show about the resolution's function?
findings.G1.inq.items.0.h: The Green New Deal resolution was introduced in the House three times and never received a House vote.
findings.G1.inq.items.0.d: The resolution was introduced as House Resolution 109 in 2019 with 101 cosponsors, as House Resolution 332 in 2021 with 104, and as House Resolution 319 in 2023 with 96. Each version was referred to committee and went no further.
findings.G1.inq.items.1.h: The only vote on the Green New Deal text was arranged by the resolution's opponents in the Senate.
findings.G1.inq.items.1.d: The Senate majority leader introduced the same text as S.J.Res. 8, and the motion to take it up failed 0 to 57, with 43 senators voting present.
findings.G1.inq.items.2.h: The Congressional Research Service describes sense-of resolutions such as the Green New Deal resolution as not legally binding.
findings.G1.inq.items.2.d: The Congressional Research Service describes sense-of measures as not legally binding because they are never presented to the President. The Service also notes that agencies may watch such measures as a signal of what Congress might do.
findings.G1.inq.open: The cosponsor counts for the three versions of the resolution come from a secondary table and should be confirmed against Congress.gov.
findings.G1.two.dec: Will members of Congress introduce binding legislation to carry out the Green New Deal resolution's climate and economic goals?
findings.G1.two.views.0.why: Climate movement organizations treat the Green New Deal resolution as an organizing framework and a commitment to which later legislation can return.
findings.G1.two.views.1.why: The resolution's sponsors can use a resolution to gather cosponsors without a cost estimate or a filibuster.
findings.G1.two.views.2.why: Opponents in Congress can bring a non-binding text such as the Green New Deal resolution up for a vote to put members on record.
findings.G3.title: Paragraph (1) of the Green New Deal resolution declares a federal duty to create a Green New Deal but assigns that duty to no agency or official.
findings.G3.plain: The resolution states that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal. It names no department, official or deadline, so no particular entity would be responsible for carrying out the duty.
findings.G3.tech: Binding mandates name an officer, as in "the Administrator shall". The phrase "the Federal Government" in paragraph (1) does not identify an entity that can be ordered, sued or funded as such.
findings.G4.title: Paragraph (2) frames the Green New Deal resolution's ten-year national mobilization with "should" and states no start date for the ten years.
findings.G4.plain: Paragraph (2) states that the resolution's goals "should be accomplished" through a ten-year national mobilization. "Should" expresses a recommendation, and the resolution does not say when the ten years begin.
findings.G4.tech: In drafting practice, "should" is hortatory. The phrase "10-year national mobilization" in paragraph (2) has no start date, and the 2021 and 2023 reintroductions carried the same ten-year language forward.
findings.G4.use: Because the resolution sets no start date, a speaker can describe the ten-year timeline as beginning at any point the speaker chooses.
findings.G5.title: Four emissions goals in paragraph (2) of the Green New Deal resolution are qualified by the words "technologically feasible", with no designated decision-maker.
findings.G5.plain: For infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture and transportation, the resolution sets a goal of removing greenhouse gas emissions "as much as technologically feasible". The resolution does not say who decides what is technologically feasible.
findings.G5.tech: In a binding statute, this qualifier hands the standard to whoever judges feasibility, and that judgment usually rests on the regulated industry's own evidence. The qualifier appears four times in the resolution, in subparagraphs (B)(i), (F), (G) and (H) of paragraph (2).
findings.G5.use: If the qualifier were carried unchanged into a binding bill, each sector's emissions goal would be only as strong as the finding of what is technologically feasible.
findings.G6.title: Paragraph (1)(A) of the Green New Deal resolution sets a net-zero greenhouse gas emissions goal with no date, baseline or accounting method in the resolving clause.
findings.G6.plain: The first goal in the resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. The resolution does not say by when the goal is to be reached, how emissions are measured, or what counts as an offset.
findings.G6.tech: The preamble cites a need for net-zero global emissions by 2050. The resolving clause links the goals to a ten-year mobilization in paragraph (2) but sets no net-zero date. The word "net" implies removals or offsets, which the resolution does not define.
findings.G6.use: Supporters and critics can each describe the net-zero target differently, and both can point to the resolution's text.
findings.G6.two.dec: Would binding legislation carrying out the Green New Deal resolution set a date for reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions?
findings.G6.two.views.0.why: Climate movement organizations would want a date for reaching net-zero emissions.
findings.G7.title: Paragraph (2)(C) of the Green New Deal resolution does not specify which energy sources qualify as "clean, renewable, and zero-emission".
findings.G7.plain: Paragraph (2)(C) calls for meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States from "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy sources. The resolution does not say whether a source must meet all three criteria or any one of them, which determines whether nuclear power qualifies.
findings.G7.tech: Nuclear generation is zero-emission but not renewable, and fossil generation with carbon capture is arguably neither. Leaving the list of qualifying sources open can keep supporters with differing views in one coalition, which is why this finding is classified as a trade-off.
findings.G7.use: The undefined category moves the decision about which energy sources qualify to whatever binding bill comes later.
findings.G8.title: Paragraph (4)(H) of the Green New Deal resolution refers to guaranteeing employment but establishes no program, eligibility rule or funding.
findings.G8.plain: Paragraph (4)(H) of the resolution speaks of "guaranteeing a job" to all people of the United States. A guarantee of employment requires a program, an employer of last resort, eligibility rules and funding, and the resolution contains none of these.
findings.G8.tech: The same is true of "guaranteeing universal access to clean water" in paragraph (2)(B)(ii) and of "providing all people of the United States with" "high-quality health care" in paragraph (4)(O). In a non-binding text, these phrases are statements of aim.
findings.G8.use: A speaker can quote the word "guaranteeing" from the resolution as if a job guarantee had been enacted.
findings.G10.title: Paragraph (2)(B)(iv) of the Green New Deal resolution calls for conditions on future infrastructure legislation that a simple resolution cannot impose.
findings.G10.plain: Paragraph (2)(B)(iv) calls for ensuring that any infrastructure bill considered by Congress addresses climate change. A statement of opinion by one chamber cannot control the content of later bills.
findings.G10.tech: A chamber can bind its own proceedings through its rules, for example by creating a point of order. A sense-of-the-House resolution is not a rule of the House.
findings.G12.title: The Green New Deal resolution's quantitative climate targets, such as the 1.5 degree Celsius warming limit, appear in the preamble, which has no operative effect.
findings.G12.plain: The resolution's specific numerical targets, such as the 1.5 degree limit and the 2050 date, appear in the "Whereas" clauses. Those clauses explain why the House is speaking and are not part of what the House resolves.
findings.G12.tech: Preambles and findings can inform interpretation but create no rights or duties. In the Green New Deal resolution, the most concrete targets appear outside the resolving clause.
findings.G12.use: Figures from the Green New Deal resolution's preamble are often quoted as if they were commitments.
findings.G9.title: The Green New Deal resolution contains no cost estimate and no authorization or appropriation of funds for its goals.
findings.G9.plain: The resolution names goals that would require very large public investment. It contains no cost figure and provides no funding, and a resolution could not provide funding.
findings.G9.tech: Only a bill or joint resolution that becomes law can authorize or appropriate funds. Paragraph (4)(A) refers to "adequate capital" through community grants, public banks and other public financing, without stating amounts.
findings.G9.use: Cost estimates for the Green New Deal from supporters and opponents cannot be checked against the resolution, because the resolution contains none.
findings.G14.title: The House did not vote on the Green New Deal resolution, and the Senate vote on a companion joint resolution failed 0 to 57.
findings.G14.plain: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate held a procedural vote on the same text, introduced by the majority leader, and it failed 0 to 57, with 43 senators voting present.
findings.G14.tech: Senate Joint Resolution 8 carried the same text as a joint resolution. Supporters of the House resolution called the vote a tactic and voted present. The episode shows how a non-binding text can be used to put members on record.
findings.G14.use: Either side can cite the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text, one as proof of no support and the other as proof of a sham process.
findings.G13.title: Separate bills introduced under the Green New Deal name, unlike House Resolution 109 itself, would carry binding provisions if enacted.
findings.G13.plain: Readers looking for measures that would change federal law should look to the separate bills introduced under the Green New Deal name, such as those on public housing and a Civilian Climate Corps.
findings.G13.tech: Those companion measures are bills (H.R. and S.), which would be binding if enacted and can be red-teamed for loopholes in the ordinary way.
bigger.lead: The Green New Deal resolution names nearly every part of the federal climate and economic agenda. Because the resolution has no legal effect, it changes none of them. The first table shows what the resolution names, and the second table shows what a binding measure would need for each goal.
bigger.map.0.note: The resolution states net-zero emissions as a goal and sets no cap, price or standard for greenhouse gas emissions.
bigger.map.1.note: The resolution calls for 100 percent clean, renewable and zero-emission power and does not define which sources qualify.
bigger.map.2.note: The resolution qualifies the emissions goal for each of these sectors by technological feasibility.
bigger.map.3.note: The resolution states no amounts or sources for public investment and financing.
bigger.map.4.note: The resolution states guarantees for jobs, wages and labor rights without creating programs to deliver them.
bigger.map.5.part: Health care, housing and economic security
bigger.map.5.note: The resolution lists health care, housing and economic security as things a Green New Deal will require.
bigger.map.6.note: Later spending and tax law on clean energy was enacted through separate bills, which sponsors of the 2023 reintroduction of the resolution cited.
stake.clim.want: Climate movement organizations want a shared framework and a public commitment to build on. Movement groups endorsed the resolution.
stake.labor.want: Labor unions want job and wage guarantees and protection for workers in industries that would shrink. Some unions endorsed the resolution.
stake.foss.role: Fossil fuel companies and their workers
stake.foss.want: Fossil fuel companies and their workers want no binding phase-out of fossil fuels or, failing that, the longest possible timeline.
stake.util.want: Electric utilities want clear rules on which power sources will count, and time to build.
stake.nuc.want: Nuclear energy advocates want nuclear power explicitly included as clean energy.
stake.fisc.role: Members of Congress focused on spending
stake.fisc.want: Members of Congress focused on spending want a cost figure and a funding source before any commitment is made.
stake.front.role: Communities named in the resolution as frontline and vulnerable
stake.front.want: Communities named in the resolution as frontline and vulnerable want an enforceable priority in investment, not only a mention in the text.
stake.spon.want: The resolution's sponsors want a statement of direction that later bills can carry out.
stake.opp.want: Opponents in Congress want a recorded vote that puts supporters of the resolution on record. The Senate vote on the Green New Deal text was arranged by the measure's opponents.
stake.crs.want: Nonpartisan congressional analysts describe sense-of resolutions as having no force of law.
stake.tex.role: A judge who reads statutes by their text
stake.tex.want: A judge who reads statutes by their text applies the words as written and will not supply what Congress left out.
stake.pur.role: A judge who reads statutes by their purpose
stake.pur.want: A judge who reads statutes by their purpose resolves doubt in favor of what the law was trying to do.
stake.olc.want: A legislative drafter wants every key term defined, every reference checked and every relationship to existing law stated.
conf_note: The Green New Deal resolution assigns no duties to any agency or official, so there is no responsible party whose independence can be assessed. A later law that carried out its goals would need this review.
